title: Normal Distribution
tagline: The bell curve — why so much data naturally clusters around the middle.
what_it_is: The normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution defined entirely by two parameters: the mean (center of the bell) and the standard deviation (width of the bell). It is the most important distribution in statistics because a huge range of real-world measurements — heights, IQ scores, measurement errors, blood pressure — naturally follow it. It is also the foundation of most classical statistical tests and the central limit theorem.
key_points: Defined by mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ). Mean sets the center, SD sets the spread.
Perfectly symmetric — mean = median = mode. The bell is identical on both sides.
The 68-95-99.7 rule: 68% of data falls within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ of the mean.
The total area under the curve = 1 (all probabilities sum to 1).
Many statistical tests assume normality — violating this assumption can invalidate results.
why_it_exists: The normal distribution emerges naturally from the central limit theorem: when you average many independent random variables, the result tends toward a normal distribution regardless of the original distribution. This is why errors in measurement, biological traits, and aggregated effects all cluster into bell shapes. Its mathematical properties make it tractable — many calculations that are impossible for other distributions have clean closed-form solutions for the normal distribution.
what_it_measures: The normal distribution describes how probable different values are for a continuous variable. The peak (at the mean) is the most probable value. Values further from the mean are progressively less probable. The standard deviation controls how quickly probability drops off — a narrow bell (small σ) means most values are close to the mean, a wide bell (large σ) means values are spread far from it.
intuition: Imagine measuring the heights of 10,000 adults. A few people are very short, a few are very tall, and the vast majority cluster around 170cm. If you plotted this as a histogram, the bars would form a bell shape — high in the middle, tapering symmetrically on both sides. This is the normal distribution. The mean is 170cm, the SD might be 10cm, which means 95% of people fall between 150cm and 190cm (within 2 SDs). The distribution tells you not just where the center is, but how confident you can be that any given person is near it.

example.text: Exam scores: mean = 70, standard deviation = 10. Distribution is approximately normal.
example.interpretation: 68% of students scored between 60 and 80. 95% scored between 50 and 90. A score of 90 is 2 standard deviations above the mean — in the top 2.5% of the class. A score of 50 is 2 SDs below the mean — in the bottom 2.5%.

breakdown.means: probability density at value x — height of the curve at that point
mean — the center of the bell
standard deviation — controls width of the bell
Euler's number ≈ 2.718 — base of natural logarithm
normalizing constant — ensures total area under curve equals 1
z-score — how many standard deviations x is from the mean

when_to_use: Use when data is continuous and you expect it to cluster symmetrically around a central value — heights, weights, measurement errors
Use the normal distribution assumption when applying t-tests, ANOVA, linear regression, and most classical statistical tests
Use z-scores to compare values from different normal distributions on a common scale
Use it to detect outliers — values beyond 3 standard deviations from the mean are flagged as anomalies
when_not_to_use: Do not assume normality for income, prices, or any quantity that cannot be negative — these are typically right-skewed
Do not use normal distribution for count data (number of events) — use Poisson distribution instead
Do not apply tests that assume normality to small samples without checking — the central limit theorem requires sufficiently large n
Do not use it for binary outcomes — use Bernoulli or binomial distributions instead
common_mistakes: Assuming all continuous data is normally distributed — checking with a histogram or Q-Q plot before applying parametric tests is essential
Confusing the probability density f(x) with probability — the density can exceed 1, only areas under the curve are probabilities
Ignoring skewness — a histogram that looks roughly bell-shaped but has a long tail is NOT normal and will violate test assumptions
Using z-scores without checking normality — z-scores are meaningful summaries of position only within a normal distribution
ds_usage: Normal distribution is assumed by linear regression (residuals should be normally distributed), t-tests, ANOVA, and many other classical methods. In feature engineering, checking whether a feature is normally distributed before applying normalization matters — log transformation is commonly applied to right-skewed features to make them more normal. In scikit-learn, StandardScaler standardizes features to have mean=0 and SD=1 (a standard normal), which is prerequisite for many algorithms like SVM and PCA. scipy.stats.norm provides pdf, cdf, and sampling functions.
